title: Philippine island fights rising seas with nature, not concrete

For years, residents of a flood-prone Philippine island north of Manila have elevated their homes atop layer upon layer of concrete, only to see floodwaters threaten them again. Burdened by strong storm surges, land subsidence and rising seas exacerbated by climate change, the 3,000 residents of tiny Pamarawan Island have turned to bamboo poles and discarded oyster shells to build a barrier aimed at weakening waves and managing floods. The unusual approach offers a nature-based alternative for a country still grappling with a multibillion-dollar scandal that drove public fury over substandard—and at times nonexistent—concrete flood-control projects. "We were terrified whenever there were typhoons. We couldn't sleep at night," fisherman Edgar Javier told AFP on a recent visit, recalling how strong waves once brought down one of his home's concrete walls. "Whenever the waves hit, the wall shakes." The project began when the city government of Malolos, home to the island, launched a study with a Dutch engineering consultancy. In this photo taken on Oct. 13, 2026, workers lay coconut-fiber nets next to bags of oyster shells on a breakwater at Pamarawan Island in Malolos City, Bulacan province. Burdened by strong storm surges, land subsidence and rising seas exacerbated by climate change, the 3,000 residents of tiny Pamarawan Island have turned to bamboo poles and discarded oyster shells to build a barrier aimed at weakening waves and managing floods. "(Concrete infrastructure) projects won't suffice," Mayor Christian Natividad told AFP. While the project, the first of its kind in the country, initially faced resistance from officials and residents working without a blueprint, Natividad said they had "nothing to lose." "It's like you accept daily flooding or you do something else with risk," he said. "I chose risk." Slowing the waves By May last year, workers, many of them residents, had begun installing bamboo poles packed with brushwood along the coast. They are designed to slow water flow and trap sediment, with the goal of gradually raising the seabed and supporting mangrove growth. When AFP journalists visited the site, workers were building an oyster-shell breakwater about 100 meters (330 feet) offshore. Under the searing heat, men in caps pounded wooden stakes used to secure coconut-fiber bags filled with shells on an artificial shore first created with sea sand. Bamboo sediment traps designed to slow water flow next to houses at Pamarawan Island in Malolos City, Bulacan province. "This breakwater's main purpose is to lessen the impact of the wave before it can reach the community," project manager Lyana Galang told AFP, adding that the oyster-shell barriers work in concert with bamboo sediment traps. Filipino scientist Antonio Contreras said the Philippines had long relied heavily on concrete dikes and seawalls , many undertaken without adequate study. "We have altered the environment so much that we tend to work against nature when in fact we should work with it," Contreras told AFP, noting that some design flaws linked to corruption had cost lives. But nature-based solutions were not a universal answer, he warned, particularly during catastrophic floods, and should complement conventional infrastructure. Contreras said the approach in Pamarawan could be replicated elsewhere, provided local environmental conditions were carefully taken into account. Bamboo and oyster shells also need to be sourced sustainably, he warned, as bamboo deteriorates over time and releases carbon as it decomposes. The nature-based installations, which cover about 14 hectares (35 acres) along Manila Bay, cost 70 million pesos ($1.1 million), including maintenance, compared with around 90 million pesos for a concrete seawall, Mayor Natividad said. He estimated bamboo will need to be replaced once every five years. Workers sew coconut-fiber bags on a breakwater at Pamarawan Island in Malolos City, Bulacan province in the Philippines. Subscribe 'Our feet are dry' With its first phase completed in late 2025, the installation has already brought some comfort to residents. Fisherman Javier said the breakwaters had softened waves and helped keep floodwaters at bay during typhoons and monsoon rains this year. "This has made a huge difference for us. We can still feel the waves, but they have significantly weakened. (They're) almost nothing now," he said. Arsenia Cabigao, 58, said flooding had previously disrupted her livelihood by submerging areas where she dried fish. "Our feet are dry at last. They weren't before," she told AFP as she sliced small fish in a narrow Pamarawan alley.
